newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND CAUTIOUS ABOUT RUSSIA-BELARUS DEAL.
newsitem.headline: POLAND CAUTIOUS ABOUT RUSSIA-BELARUS DEAL.

text.p: Poland reacted with a mix of caution and concern on Thursday to the scaled-down Union Treaty between Russia and Belarus, its sometimes troublesome neighbours.
The foreign ministry said the agreement was merely another failed attempt to bring the two countries closer, which posed no immediate threat to Poland.

"In a short-term perspective, I can see no immediate threat, no significant change. Russia and Belarus have twice came close to signing documents aimed at closer cooperation or integration," the ministry's spokswoman Pawel Dobrowolski said.
He added that it was in Poland's interests that Belarus maintain independence and sovreignty.
But parliament's foreign policy commitee head Bronislaw Geremek said he was wary about the longer-term implications of the agreement.
"From the point of view of European security..., it is difficult not to worry, because Russia's military might will appear on the Polish-Belarus border," PAP news agency quoted Geremek as saying.
The deal between Russia and Belarus, signed on Wednesday, was a three-page, watered-down version of the origianl 17-page draft, which had provided for integration between the two states.

The accord, scaled down after intervention by Russian liberals fearful of integration, provided for freedom of movement and rights of residency, property ownership and participation in local elections in both Belarus and Russia.
An accompanying charter, containing the meat of the original draft, was merely initialled by the two presidents and sent for six weeks of reworking and public discussion.
Some Polish politicians said the deal between Moscow and Minsk was a warning to NATO against recruiting new members from eastern Europe.
"It is an attempt to frighten (Western countries)," said Romuald Szeremietiew, a former defense minister and the leader of right-wing Movement for the Republic party.
Russia opposes plans of Poland and other former Soviet bloc countries to join the Western military alliance, saying this would put its national security under threat.
Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko, vehemently critical of the enlargement, has recently accused Poland of harbouring Belarus opposition activists, who want to oust him from office.
He has suggested, without elaborating, that the Polish minority in Belarus was being manipulated into actions against his administration.
